raw_text:
The rover had hit the sinkhole nose first, a grinding shriek of metal followed by a sudden, gut wrenching stop. Smoke and the acrid smell of burnt circuits filled the cabin. Sam was wedged under the control panel, his leg twisted at an angle that made his stomach turn. He fought the blackness that swam at the edge of his vision and clawed his way free. A few feet away, Ben was slumped against the shattered viewport, a nasty gash on his forehead bleeding freely into his bright red hair.

Sam scrambled over to him and shook his shoulder. "Ben! Hey, Ben! Wake up!"

The younger man groaned and his eyelids fluttered. "My head," he moaned. "Feels like a power hammer." He touched the cut on his scalp and winced. "What happened? Did we make it?"

"We made it through the pass," Sam grunted, hauling Ben upright. "The landing could have been better. Come on, we have to get out of here before the whole thing blows."

He kicked open the warped side hatch and bundled them both out into the biting wind of the salt flats. They collapsed onto the cracked white earth, gasping for breath. The wreck of their rover hissed and popped behind them.

"Some driving, Sam!" Ben said, trying for a weak grin. "You almost got us killed!"

"Almost is the important word," Sam retorted, wiping grime from his face with the back of his hand. "Besides, I was a little busy dodging pulse cannon fire. Next time, you can do the flying."

"Ha! Fat chance," Ben coughed. "They'd have shot us down before we even cleared the city wall. You did great, Sam. Honest! We're alive, aren't we?"

"For now," Sam muttered, his eyes scanning the desolate horizon. "I was just hoping for a quieter reception. Now get that bleeding stopped before you...." He broke off, his body going rigid.

A group of figures was approaching from the east, their shapes shimmering in the heat haze. They were moving fast, their long-limbed strides eating up the ground. As they got closer, Sam could see the glint of sunlight on rifle barrels. They wore the patched brown cloaks of desert nomads, but their weapons were corporate issue.

"Oh, no," Ben breathed. "Not them."

"They think we're from the Authority," Sam said, his mind racing. "They must have seen us come down. They're not going to be friendly."

One of the figures raised a rifle and a searing bolt of energy hissed past Sam's ear. He grabbed Ben by the collar and shoved him behind his own body, throwing his hands up in the air.

"Hold your fire!" he yelled, his voice sounding thin in the vast emptiness. "We're not with the Authority! We're fugitives! We just escaped!"

The nomads swarmed around them, leveling their rifles. They were a hard looking bunch. Their faces were hidden behind dust goggles and scarves, and their eyes were cold and suspicious. The leader, a tall woman with a cruel looking vibroknife strapped to her thigh, stepped forward until the muzzle of her rifle was inches from Sam's chest.

"Fugitives?" she rasped, her voice like grinding stones. "You fly an Authority skimmer. You wear Authority clothes. You are spies."

"Wait, listen!" Sam pleaded. "It's a long story! We stole the skimmer. We have information! We know their patrol routes, their supply weaknesses. We have to get this to the Resistance!"

The leader's eyes narrowed. The nomads behind her muttered and shifted their grips on their rifles, their hostility a palpable force. Sam felt a drop of sweat trickle down his temple. Ben suddenly pushed himself forward, shoving past Sam. He jabbed a finger at the woman's chest, his fear forgotten in a blaze of anger.

"Listen to him, you sand-eater!" Ben shouted. "Use your brain! Do we look like spies? We just risked our necks getting through the cannon blockade! We have a datachip with the Authority's entire security roster for this sector. We need to get it to Commander Joric! He'll want to hear how his so called allies nearly shot the messengers! Now, are you going to take us to him, or are you going to stand here and let the Authority's trackers find us all?"

A slow, dangerous smile spread across the woman's lips, visible even behind her scarf. She lowered her rifle a few inches.

"The little one has fire," she said to the man next to her. He chuckled. "Maybe they are not spies. They are too noisy to be spies. But you were very close to being dead, little one. The Authority has given us much grief this week."

"So help us give it back to them," Ben said quickly. "Where is Joric? Can you hold them off?"

The woman's smile vanished. She looked out across the flats, her gaze distant and tired. "Joric is far from here. The Authority pushes hard. They have new walkers, new cannons. We lose ground every day. There are no other cells in this sector. Only us. And we are not enough. We do not have the guns, or the power packs. And skimmers? Look at the sky! It is full of their patrol drones. Yes, it looks very bad. But we do not run. Come. I will take you to my camp. We will see about this datachip."

She turned and started walking without another word, her rifle held loosely in one hand. Sam and Ben fell into step with the rest of the nomads, a silent, grim procession across the white salt. The silence was broken only by the crunch of their boots and the distant, mournful howl of the wind.

Sam leaned close to Ben. "Nice work," he whispered. "For a minute there, I thought we were finished."

"I was just getting started," Ben whispered back, though his voice lacked its earlier fire. "I just hope this Joric is real. I just hope there's someone left to give this information to."

Sam did not answer. He felt a deep weariness settle into his bones, a weight heavier than any fatigue from the crash. The image of the Authority's endless legions, their gleaming chrome and perfect formations, was burned into his mind. They were a steel river, and these nomads were just a few stones in their path.

At the edge of the flats, the nomads led them into a deep, twisting canyon. In a hidden alcove, sheltered from the wind and prying eyes, was their camp. It was a sorry collection of tents made from scavenged materials. A dozen or so more people, old men and young children, looked up with hollow eyes as they entered. The woman led them to the largest tent and stopped before a grizzled man cleaning a rifle.

"Kael," she said. "These two fell out of the sky. They say they have information for Joric."

The man, Kael, looked up. His eyes were bleak and exhausted, but a flicker of interest sparked within them. "Information?" he asked, his voice rough.

Ben did the talking. He spoke quickly and clearly, explaining their escape, the stolen skimmer, and the datachip. Kael listened without interruption, his expression unreadable. When Ben finished, Kael held out a calloused hand.

"Let me see it."

Ben hesitated for a second, then pulled a small, silver chip from his pocket and placed it in the man's palm. Kael stared at it for a long moment, then rose and walked to a battered looking console in the corner of the tent. He slid the chip into a slot. Lines of code scrolled rapidly across the screen.

Kael's back was to them, but Sam saw his shoulders straighten. He leaned closer to the screen, his whole body tense with concentration.

"It's real," he breathed, turning to face them. A new light shone in his dead eyes, a hard, sharp gleam of hope. "It's all here. Patrol routes. Fueling stations. Command codes. You have done a brave thing, boys."

Ben flushed, looking down at his feet. "We just wanted to do what was right," he said.

Kael’s lips twisted into something that might have been a smile. "With this," he said, tapping the screen, "we can do more than just hide. We can finally fight back."

raw_text:
I would give much for that, Ben. And perhaps you will." He gestured toward the screen where a schematic of a pipeline network was now displayed. "The Authority runs on energy. They bleed our world dry to fuel their war machine. Their armies, their ships, their cities, all of it flows through conduits like these. And right here," he tapped a blinking junction point on the map, "is Pumping Station 7. It is the heart of this entire sector's power grid."

The woman who had found them, the one Kael had called Mara, stepped forward. Her face was grim, her eyes hard. "We know of the station, Kael. It is guarded by a full garrison. To attack it is suicide."

"It was suicide yesterday," Kael corrected her, his voice low and intense. "But yesterday we did not have this." He jabbed a finger at the datachip still sitting in the console. "These boys brought us the access codes. The patrol schedules. The service hatches. For the first time, Mara, we do not have to smash our fists against the front gate. We can slip a knife between the ribs."

A murmur went through the small group gathered in the tent. It was a sound mixed of fear and a desperate, unfamiliar hope. Sam watched them, these tattered ghosts of the salt flats. Their clothes were patched, their faces were lined with worry and grime, but in their eyes he saw the same fire he had seen in the Belgians. It was the fire of a people pushed too far, a people with nothing left to lose.

"What is the plan?" Ben asked, his voice barely a whisper but cutting through the tension. He stood straighter, his weariness seemingly forgotten. He was no longer the boy who had crash landed a skimmer, but a soldier asking for his orders.

Kael turned his gaze on Ben, and a slow, approving nod was his answer. "The plan is simple, and therefore dangerous. A small team will use a service tunnel shown on this map. It comes up inside the station's primary cooling conduit. We use the codes to bypass the internal sentries, plant our charges on the main turbines, and get out. If we are successful, this entire sector goes dark. The Authority's patrols will be grounded. Their defenses will be blind. It will give us time. It will give our allies time."

"Allies?" Sam spoke up, the word tasting strange on his lips. "There are others?"

Kael's mouth tightened. "There are other pockets of resistance. We call ourselves the Free Clans. We are scattered. We fight, we hide, we survive. But we have no way to speak to one another, no way to coordinate. If we can knock out their power grid, even for a day, we can use the blackout to move. To regroup. This is more than just a raid, boys. This is the signal."

An old man with a stringy white beard, who had been silent until now, shuffled forward. "It is a fool's errand, Kael! You are sending our best fighters to their deaths on the word of two strangers who fell from the sky. What if it is a trap? The Authority is cunning."

"Silas is right to be cautious," Kael said, his tone even. "But I have looked at this data. I have lived my life reading the Authority's signs, and I tell you this is real. This is our one chance. A chance I am willing to risk my own life for." He looked around the tent, his eyes meeting each of theirs in turn. "I will lead the raid myself. I need six volunteers."

Before anyone else could speak, Ben stepped forward again. "I will go."

Sam grabbed his arm. "Ben, no!" he hissed. "You heard the man. This is a suicide mission. We've done our part."

"He said they needed every hand that could hold a rifle," Ben shot back, his eyes flashing. "We started this, Sam. We have to see it through. We can't just hand them the map and then run and hide while they die for us."

"We're pilots, Ben, not saboteurs!" Sam argued, his voice rising in desperation. "We wouldn't know the first thing about planting charges or fighting in tunnels!"

"Then we will learn!" Ben pulled his arm free from Sam's grasp. He looked at Kael. "We have seen the inside of an Authority command center. We know their protocols. We know how their soldiers talk, how they move. We can be useful."

Kael studied the two of them, his gaze moving from Ben's fiery determination to Sam's frantic pleading. He looked like the Belgian corporal, a man made old and tired by a war that had come to his home. "The young one has the heart of a lion," he said to Sam. "And you have the sense of a good brother. Both are valuable. But he is right. You know the enemy in a way we do not. Your presence could be the thing that keeps us from making a fatal mistake." He paused, his gaze heavy. "The risk is great. I will not order you to go. But if you volunteer, you will be welcome."

Sam looked at Ben's set jaw and the unshakeable resolve in his eyes. He saw the same look Freddy had when he dressed down the Belgian soldiers. It was a look that would not be denied. Sam's shoulders slumped. He felt that same crushing weariness return, the weight of a world that kept demanding more than he had to give. He gave a short, bitter laugh. "It seems I don't have much of a choice, do I? If he goes, I go."

"Good," Kael grunted. He turned to the others. Mara stepped forward without a word. Two other grim faced men and a young, wiry woman followed suit. The team was assembled. "Get what rest you can," Kael commanded. "We move in two hours, under the cover of the twin moons."

The two hours passed in a blur of frantic preparation. There was no time for rest. Sam and Ben were handed scavenged energy rifles, heavy and poorly balanced compared to the sleek Authority weapons they were used to. Mara showed them how to check the charge and clear a jam, her movements quick and efficient. She did not waste words. She demonstrated once, then watched with critical eyes as they repeated the action. "You do it slow, you die," she said simply, and moved on.

They were given strips of dried meat and a canteen of brackish, metallic tasting water. Sam ate because he knew he needed the strength, but the food tasted like ash in his mouth. He watched Ben, who was practically vibrating with a nervous energy. The younger man was cleaning his rifle with a focus Sam had only ever seen him apply to a starship's flight stick. He was in his element, ready for a fight. Sam just felt sick.

Soon enough, Kael gathered them. They were a small, pathetic looking assault team. Seven figures in rags, armed with scavenged gear, setting off to challenge an empire. They piled into the back of a large, flatbed desert transport, a relic from before the Authority's conquest. Its engine coughed to life with a belch of black smoke, and it rumbled out of the canyon onto the salt flats.

The ride was bone jarring and cold. The twin moons cast long, distorted shadows across the white expanse, making the world look alien and hostile. No one spoke. The only sound was the roar of the ancient engine and the wind whipping past their ears. Sam huddled deeper into his threadbare jacket, his rifle clutched in his numb fingers. He looked over at Ben, whose face was turned up toward the star-dusted sky, a look of grim wonder on his face. What was he thinking? Was he not scared? Sam was terrified. He felt like a fraud, a pilot who had no business holding a gun, heading toward a fight he had no chance of winning.

After what felt like an eternity, Kael pounded on the roof of the cab. The transport slowed and veered off the main flats, pulling behind a towering rock formation. "This is as far as the truck goes," Kael announced as they all jumped down. "The rest is on foot. From here on, absolute silence."

He led them on a weaving path through a maze of rocks and dry gulches. The ground was treacherous, covered in loose scree that threatened to slide and give away their position with every step. They moved slowly, carefully, like wraiths in the moonlight. Ahead, Sam could see the faint, pulsing glow of Pumping Station 7. It squatted on the horizon like a monstrous metal spider, a web of pipelines and conduits radiating from its central body. Searchlights swept across the desert in lazy, overlapping arcs.

"There," Kael whispered, pointing to a spot at the base of a massive pipeline. "The service tunnel. The schematics say the access hatch is twenty meters east of that support pylon."

They crept forward, keeping low, using the shadows of the rocks for cover. The air grew thick with the low thrum of the station's machinery. It was a constant, deep hum that vibrated in Sam's teeth. They reached the pylon and fanned out, their rifles up, scanning the darkness. Mara found the hatch, a simple metal plate nearly invisible against the dark ground. One of the other men, a hulking giant named Gregor, pried it open with a crowbar. The screech of metal was terrifyingly loud in the silence. They all froze, but no alarms sounded.

Kael dropped a rope into the blackness and then disappeared down it without a sound. One by one, the others followed. Sam's heart was a frantic drum against his ribs. This was it. There was no turning back. He took one last look at the open sky, then swung his legs into the hole and began to descend into the earth.

The tunnel was narrow and smelled of ozone and stale, recycled air. It was a maintenance crawlspace, never meant for men to fight in. They moved in single file, their shoulders brushing the cold metal walls. Ben was directly in front of Sam, his breathing quick and shallow. Kael was in the lead, a small datapad in his hand displaying the schematic from the chip.

"Internal sensor grid ahead," Kael breathed, his voice echoing slightly in the confined space. "The code should create a temporary blind spot for thirty seconds. When I give the word, we run. Ready?"

A series of tense grunts was his reply. They crouched in the darkness, waiting. Sam could feel the hum of the station more intensely now. It was all around them, a living presence.

"Now!" Kael hissed.

They sprinted. The tunnel floor was slick with condensation, and Sam nearly lost his footing twice. He could see a heavy bulkhead door at the far end of the corridor. Twenty seconds. Ten. They were almost there. Kael was already at the door's control panel, his fingers flying across the keys. With five seconds to spare, the heavy door slid open with a hiss of pneumatics. They scrambled through, and Kael slammed it shut behind them just as a red light began to flash at the far end of the tunnel they had just left.

"Too close," Mara muttered, leaning against the wall to catch her breath.

"Luck is with us so far," Kael said, though he did not sound convinced. "We are inside the cooling conduit network. The main turbine chamber is two levels down. Follow me. Watch your step."

They were in a much larger space now, a catwalk overlooking a vast, cavernous chamber filled with enormous pipes. The air was hot and humid, and the noise was deafening, a symphony of whirring machinery and rushing water. They moved quickly along the catwalk, the metal grates rattling under their boots.

They had just reached a spiral staircase leading down when it happened. A voice, cold and metallic, echoed through the chamber. "Unauthorized entry detected in sector Gamma. All units converge."

Kael swore under his breath. "The code didn't hold! It must have been a trap!"

"Or they are better than we thought," Mara said, her rifle already at her shoulder.

From a doorway on the far side of the chamber, two Authority sentinels emerged. They were not human. They were gleaming chrome machines, seven feet tall, with glowing red optics and rifles built into their arms. "Intruders identified," one of them boomed. "Lethal force authorized."

The first shots were bolts of searing red energy that sizzled past their heads and struck the wall behind them, leaving molten craters in the metal. Kael and Mara returned fire, their less powerful bolts splashing harmlessly off the sentinels' armor. "Their chests!" Kael yelled over the din. "Aim for the central processor!"

Gregor, the giant, let out a roar and charged, firing his rifle from the hip. One of the sentinels turned its attention to him. A red bolt caught him square in the chest. He stumbled, a look of surprise on his face, then fell from the catwalk into the darkness below.

"Gregor!" the young woman cried out.

"No time for that!" Kael shouted. "Keep firing!"

Sam was frozen, his back pressed against the railing. His mind was blank with terror. This was not like a dogfight in space. There was no maneuvering, no clever piloting. It was just noise and light and death. Ben grabbed his shoulder and shook him, hard. "Sam, shoot! You have to shoot!"

Ben's voice broke through the panic. Sam raised his rifle on trembling arms, sighted on the nearest sentinel, and pulled the trigger. The bolt went wide. He fired again, and again. One of his shots struck the sentinel's shoulder, causing it to stagger. Ben let out a whoop. "You did it, Sam! Again!"

Emboldened, Sam aimed more carefully. He and Ben fired together, a coordinated volley. Their combined fire, along with Kael's and Mara's, began to have an effect. The first sentinel's chest plate began to glow cherry red. With a final, well placed shot from Mara, it exploded in a shower of sparks and shrapnel.

The second sentinel swung its weapon toward them, but before it could fire, one of Kael's team, a man named Rhys, leaped onto its back from the staircase above. He held a wicked looking blade, a sharpened piece of scrap metal. He plunged it deep into the joint between the sentinel's head and torso. The machine thrashed wildly, trying to shake him, but Rhys held on like a bulldog. The sentinel's red eye flickered, and then it went dark. It crumpled to the ground, taking Rhys with it.

They rushed to his side. He was alive, but his leg was trapped under the machine's weight, and it was bent at a horrifying angle. "Go," Rhys gasped, his face pale with pain. "Finish the mission. Don't let this be for nothing."

Kael hesitated for a fraction of a second. "Mara, stay with him. Get him free if you can. The rest of you, with me!"

There was no time to argue. They left Mara and the injured Rhys and plunged down the staircase. The turbine chamber was just below. It was a massive, cylindrical room dominated by three colossal turbines, spinning so fast they were just a blur. The noise was a physical blow.

"The charges!" Kael yelled, handing a satchel to Sam and another to the young woman, Elara. "On the primary axle housing of each turbine! Ben, you're with me! Cover us!"

Sam's hands were clumsy as he pulled out the magnetic charge. It was heavy and had a simple timer on it. He scrambled onto the base of the nearest turbine, the whole structure vibrating so intensely he felt like his teeth would shake loose. He found the axle housing, a thick cylinder of metal, and slapped the charge into place. He armed it, the small display blinking a ten minute countdown.

He looked up. Elara had her charge placed. Kael and Ben were providing cover fire, pinning down two human Authority guards who had appeared on an upper gantry. Sam scrambled back to join them. "First one is set!" he yelled.

"Good work!" Kael shouted back. "Now let's get out of here!"

They fell back toward the staircase, but their path was blocked. Four more guards had come up from the level below. They were trapped. "This way!" Ben yelled, pointing to a narrow maintenance ladder that ran up the side of the turbine housing. "It's our only shot!"

It was a desperate gamble, but they had no other choice. Kael went first, then Elara. Sam pushed Ben toward the ladder. "Go!" Ben scrambled up. Sam was about to follow when a searing pain erupted in his shoulder. He cried out and fell to his knees. A lucky shot from one of the guards had grazed him. His arm was numb, useless.

"Sam!" Ben screamed from the ladder.

Sam looked up. The guards were advancing. The countdown on the charges was at seven minutes. "Go, Ben!" he yelled, his voice raw. "Get out of here! That's an order!"

"I'm not leaving you!" Ben shouted back, and he started to climb back down.

"You fool!" Sam gasped, trying to get to his feet. But Ben was a whirlwind of motion. He didn't climb down. He leaped. He landed on one of the guards, knocking him over. He came up with the guard's pistol in his hand and fired twice, taking down a second guard before anyone could react. It was the most insane, reckless, beautiful thing Sam had ever seen.

The remaining two guards turned their fire on Ben. Kael, from his position on the ladder, laid down a covering fire that forced them back. It gave Sam the opening he needed. He staggered to his feet, clutching his wounded shoulder, and scrambled up the ladder after Elara. Ben was right behind him, his face flushed with the thrill of battle. "See?" he panted as he caught up. "Told you I could be useful!"

Sam didn't have the breath to reply. They reached the top of the ladder and found themselves on another catwalk. This one led to a different exit tunnel, one marked on Kael's datapad as an emergency exhaust vent. They ran, the sounds of the firefight fading behind them.

They burst out into the cool night air, emerging from a vent halfway up a rocky cliff face, a good hundred meters from the station. They didn't stop. They scrambled down the rocks and ran until their lungs burned and their legs were jelly. Only then did they collapse behind a ridge and look back.

Dave and Freddy gave the lieutenant a quick nod of thanks. The young officer was already turning back to his men, shouting an order to shift a machine gun a few feet to the left. There was no time for long goodbyes. War did not wait for such things. They followed the corporal back through the trees and onto the winding dirt road. The sounds of battle seemed louder now, a constant, hungry rumble that vibrated up through the soles of their shoes.

The scene on the road had changed in the few minutes they had been in the woods. Before, it had been empty. Now, a slow, sad trickle of people was shuffling westward, away from the noise. An old woman with a face like a dried apple pushed a wheelbarrow piled high with lumpy sacks and a brass clock. Two small children, their faces streaked with tears and dirt, clung to her skirt. A man with one arm in a bloody sling led a tired looking cow by a rope. Nobody spoke. They just moved, their eyes fixed on the road ahead, their faces empty of everything but fear and exhaustion.

"Gosh, Freddy," Dave murmured, his throat suddenly tight. "Look at them all. It's just awful."

Freddy's jaw was set in a hard line. He watched the refugees shuffle past, his own tiredness forgotten for a moment. "This is what they do, Dave. This is the result of those Stukas and tanks. It's why we have to get our information through. We have to stop this."

The Belgian corporal trudged along beside them, his rifle held loosely in his hand. He grunted in agreement. "They come from the villages to the east," he said, his voice flat. "There are no villages there anymore. Only fire. And the Boche." He spat on the ground. "They move very fast."

They walked in silence for another ten minutes, the rumble of the front growing into a series of distinct, jarring thuds and cracks. The air smelled of smoke and turned earth. Suddenly, a new sound cut through the din. It was a high pitched, thin wail that grew in volume with terrifying speed. It was a noise that scraped at the nerves and turned the blood to ice.

"Stukas!" the corporal yelled, his voice cracking. "Down! Into the ditch!"

He didn't have to say it twice. Dave and Freddy flung themselves off the road and into a shallow, weed choked ditch. The corporal landed right beside them. The wailing sound became an unholy shriek as the dive bomber plunged toward the earth. Dave buried his face in his arms, his heart hammering against his ribs so hard he thought it would break right through. The world seemed to hold its breath.

Then came the explosion. It was not one sound, but a whole series of them. The ground leaped up and slammed into Dave's body. A giant fist of air pressure punched his ears. Dirt and stones rained down on them. A second explosion followed, just as close, and then a third, farther away. The shrieking of the planes receded, replaced by the crackle of fire and the screams of the wounded out on the road.

Slowly, Dave lifted his head. His ears were ringing. A thick cloud of black smoke was billowing up from a spot on the road just a hundred yards ahead. The old woman's wheelbarrow was a twisted wreck, its contents scattered. The cow lay on its side, kicking its legs feebly. The corporal was already on his feet, peering out from the ditch.

"They are gone," he said. "For now." He looked at the carnage on the road and a string of angry French words burst from his lips. He crossed himself quickly. "Come. We cannot help them. We must keep moving."

They scrambled out of the ditch, their clothes and faces caked with fresh dirt. Dave felt sick to his stomach. He had seen planes fight in the air, but this was different. This was cold-blooded murder from the sky. He found himself shaking, and was angry about it.

Freddy clapped him on the shoulder. "Steady on, Dave," he said, though his own face was pale as a sheet. "We're all right. We just have to keep going."

They hurried on, their pace quickened by the fresh horror. The dirt road soon met a wider, paved one. Here the chaos was a thousand times worse. The road was a solid jam of military vehicles, all pointing west. Trucks, cannons, staff cars, and ambulances were tangled together in a hopeless knot. Soldiers shouted and cursed, trying to clear a path. Other soldiers simply sat on the running boards of their trucks, their rifles across their laps, their faces dazed and defeated. A column of thick, oily smoke in a field nearby marked the grave of a French tank.

The corporal took one look at the mess and shook his head. "It is no good. We will never find a vehicle here. We go on foot. It will be faster."

He led them off the road and into the fields, cutting across muddy pastures and jumping over fences. They kept the choked road in sight, using it as a guide. For more than an hour they trudged on, their legs aching, their throats parched. The sounds of fighting were all around them now, small arms fire mixing with the boom of artillery. Twice more they had to dive for cover as German planes strafed the road, their machine guns spitting fire.

At last, the corporal pointed to a cluster of stone buildings set back from the road. It was a large farmhouse with a big barn and several outbuildings. A Belgian flag hung limply from a makeshift pole on the roof. "There," he panted. "Battalion Command Post. We are here."

As they got closer, they saw that the farm was a hive of frantic activity. Wounded men lay on bloody straw just inside the open doors of the barn, tended by a single, overworked medic. Officers with maps in their hands hurried back and forth across the muddy courtyard. A field telephone buzzed incessantly from an open window in the farmhouse. This was not a headquarters. It was a place of desperate, last ditch command.

Their corporal seemed to know his way. He led them straight into the main farmhouse and pushed through a crowded hallway. "Major Claes!" he called out. "I have two men for Major Claes! With urgent intelligence from the Lieutenant in the woods!"

A grizzled officer with a dirty bandage wrapped around his head turned from a large map tacked to the wall. His eyes were red rimmed and furious. "What is it? What now? Can't you see we are busy?"

"My Major," the corporal said, saluting. "These two boys. They are an American and an Englishman. They escaped from the Boche. They have seen the German battle maps. The Lieutenant said you must hear their report."

Major Claes's angry expression was replaced by one of sharp curiosity. He stared at Dave and Freddy, taking in their torn flight suits and grime-caked faces. "Is this true? You have escaped from Germany?"

Freddy stepped forward. "Yes, sir. We stole a plane. We have information from a German command post map. It's about their main attack."

"Show me," the Major commanded, turning back to his own map. "Show me what you saw."

Freddy moved to the map, with Dave right behind him. The map showed Belgium and northern France. It was covered in red and blue pencil marks, a confusing scrawl of battle lines that seemed to be moving in only one direction.

"We saw their map just yesterday, sir," Freddy explained, his finger hovering over the paper. "It was covered in pins and flags. They weren't all pointed here, at the Albert Canal. The biggest concentration, the main spearhead, was much farther south. There was a whole line of pins here." His finger traced a line through the dense green area marked 'Ardennes Forest'. "They were aimed right for here. For Sedan."

Major Claes stared at Freddy's finger, then at the map. He went utterly still. The color drained from his face, leaving it a pasty grey under the dirt and the bandage. He whispered a single word, a French curse. "Sedan." Then he looked at his own map again, at the reports of enemy breakthroughs on his southern flank that had seemed so minor an hour ago. "Sacrebleu," he breathed. "It is not a push. It is a swing. They are trying to cut us all off!"

He spun around from the map and grabbed the field telephone from the hands of a startled radio operator. "Get me Division! Now!" he roared into the mouthpiece. He listened for a second, then roared again. "I do not care if he is with the General! This is more important!" He turned away from the phone for a second and jabbed a finger at a young aide. "You! Find a car! Anything that runs! A motorcycle, a bicycle, I don't care! These two boys must get to Chateau de Villes. To G.H.Q. The General must hear this from their own lips! Go, now!"

The aide scurried away. Major Claes turned back to the phone, his voice a torrent of urgent French. Dave and Freddy stood there, suddenly the center of a storm they had created. They exchanged a look. Maybe, just maybe, they were not too late.

A few minutes later, the aide returned, breathless. "A car, Major! A Citroen. The driver is waiting."

Major Claes slammed the phone down. He strode over to Dave and Freddy and put a heavy hand on each of their shoulders. His eyes, though exhausted, burned with a new fire. "You have done a great service for Belgium. For all the Allies. Now you must do one more. You must tell the General what you have told me. Go with God."

He pushed them toward the door. The corporal who had guided them gave them a final, hopeful nod. "God be with you, my little ones," he said, his voice thick with emotion. "And may your news do some good."

They were hustled out into the courtyard and into the back of a small, black staff car. The driver was a boy no older than they were, with a pale face and knuckles that were white on the steering wheel. Without a word, he gunned the engine and the car leaped forward, skidding in the mud before finding purchase on the road.

The drive was a nightmare. The young Belgian drove like a madman, swerving around abandoned trucks and shell craters. The paved road was a testament to the totality of the German assault. Here and there, they passed the blackened husks of tanks and armored cars, some Belgian, some French, and a few German. The air was thick with the stench of burning rubber and something else, something sweet and horrible that Dave didn't want to identify. The roar of battle was no longer in the distance. It was here, on either side of them, a constant, deafening symphony of destruction.

After what felt like an eternity, the driver swerved off the main road and onto a long, tree lined lane. At the end of it stood a magnificent old chateau, a fairy tale castle of grey stone and steep slate roofs. Chateau de Villes. But the fairy tale was over. The lawn was chewed up by truck tires. In the main courtyard, soldiers were feeding stacks of paper into a bonfire. Men were loading heavy crates onto trucks with a desperate haste. It was clear at a glance. They were evacuating. They were almost too late.
